title: VIALS-AA: different paths to scientific image reasoning
summary: Independent VIALS-AA results, interactive agent traces, and an analysis of how models inspect scientific images.
body:
# VIALS-AA: different paths to scientific image reasoning

VIALS-AA is our implementation of Handshake AI's VIALS benchmark, testing whether language models can interpret scientific images and answer questions about the evidence they contain. Models take different paths to a correct answer, and often get questions wrong even after extensively inspecting the images.

VIALS-AA leaderboard Read the methodology Explore the traces

This is the launch article and shows VIALS-AA results as of November 6, 2026. For current results, see the VIALS-AA leaderboard .

VIALS-AA tests whether models can interpret scientific images and answer questions about the evidence they contain. We run each of its 161 tasks three times with Stirrup , our open source reference harness, giving models code execution and image inspection tools. The results show differences in both reliable task success and the amount of work models do to reach an answer.

- Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads with a score of 64% . It answers all three repeats correctly on 103 of 161 tasks, two more than GPT-6 Astra (max). Gemini 4 Carbon (high), GPT-6 Luna (max), GPT-6.1 Sol (max), GPT-6.1 Terra (max), and GPT-6 Astra (max) make up the score–cost Pareto frontier among the models tested

- More turns and visual inspection don't always get better results. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, with fallback) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) score similarly on VIALS-AA ( 60% and 59% , respectively), but Claude Sonnet 5.5 makes 3.6 × as many tool calls per task

- Consistency separates models with similar pass@3 rates. Kimi K3.1 Pro (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) each solve around three-quarters of tasks at least once. Requiring all three repeats to succeed separates their scores: 45% for Kimi K3.1 Pro (max) versus 63% for GPT-6 Astra (max). We require all three because a result that changes between runs cannot be relied on in scientific work

- Cost per task varies nearly 99 ×. It ranges from 0.02 for GPT-6 Luna (max) to 1.77 for Grok 4.7 (xhigh). GPT-6.1 Sol (max) scores 59% at 0.06 per task, about a thirtieth of the cost of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, with fallback) for similar performance ( 61% )

Share of tasks answered correctly in all three repeats (pass3)

No publicly available API

### VIALS-AA: Score vs. Cost per Task

VIALS-AA Score · Cost per task (USD)

Most attractive quadrant

Cost is calculated from input, cache-read, cache-write, reasoning, and answer token prices, divided by the task count. Token usage is averaged across the 3 independent repeats per task, using each model's representative cache hit rate. Costs include contestant model calls only; judge calls are excluded.

## Example trajectories: different paths through scientific images

The first task asks models to locate protein spot 22 in a gel electrophoresis image and estimate its molecular-weight range from the vertical axis. Models take different paths: a short visual inspection, explicit measurement, or repeated checks using annotations and processed views. With Grok 4.7 (xhigh), we see extensive inspection and annotation still end in a wrong answer.

## Short inspection and explicit measurement can both work

### Short visual inspection

GPT-6 Astra (max) checks the image dimensions, opens the original, makes a 4× enlargement, and opens it. It then writes the correct answer and finishes in six turns. It makes no pixel measurements or contrast adjustments and draws no reference lines, relying on its visual accuracy to answer correctly without additional tool use.

### Explicit measurement and calculation

Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) enlarges the gel and crops the region around spot 22. It measures the ladder bands, inspects pixels near the arrow, draws reference lines, enhances contrast, and interpolates molecular weight. These explicit measurements check the spot's position against the ladder and support the 40-50 kDa answer. It finishes in 18 turns.

### Repeated checks (that end in a visual error)

Grok 4.7 (xhigh) repeatedly checks the region using grids, thresholds, reference lines, and labeled pixels. It uses 27 turns and 20 image views, but answers 50-70 kDa . In its final annotated view, Grok circles the printed “22” in orange and the arrow tip in red, placing the tip on its green 50 kDa guide. Its final answer cites the label and leader to justify 50-70 kDa. This suggests it anchors the range on the annotation rather than the faint protein spot. Interpolation by Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) separates the label (about 53 kDa) from the spot (about 48.7 kDa), supporting the reference range of 40-50 kDa.

## Interpreting images without native vision

Vision-enabled models are a natural fit for VIALS-AA: they can inspect a scientific figure, read its labels, and relate visual features to the question. We also wanted to test how a model without native vision would approach these tasks. We gave GLM-5.3 (max) the same image files and code execution, allowing it to investigate the figure through tools.

Without native vision, the model relies on code to extract evidence from the image. In the spot-22 trajectory below, GLM-5.3 (max) loads the image into arrays, enlarges and thresholds regions for OCR, compares pixel intensities, and prints coordinates and text maps of the image. It uses those outputs to locate labels, measure the molecular-weight scale, and choose a candidate spot. Each round of code returns another piece of evidence for the model to interpret and refine.

This selected pair shows the extra work involved, along with its limits. GLM-5.3-Flash (max) combines code with ten image views and finishes in 30 turns with the correct range. GLM-5.3 (max) takes 54 turns and 57 code calls, with no image views, and answers incorrectly.

## Tool usage differs vastly between models

We classified tool calls across all 19 models in our original test set, covering 9,177 rollouts. Most calls were about visual evidence. 38.3% of tool calls were viewing images, while 47.3% prepared or measured them , creating crops, enhancing views, and extracting measurements from pixels. Image measurement accounted for just 5–6% of tool calls for GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), compared with 25–27% for Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max).

### VIALS-AA: Tool Calls per Task

Mean tool calls per task, averaged over three independent repeats

Calls that finish or abandon the task are excluded from tool-call counts. Per-task values are averaged across recorded repeats, with up to 483 observations per model. Tool calls per turn is the total number of counted tool calls divided by the total number of completed model turns. Repeats without a recorded turn count, such as an immediate safety block, are excluded.

#### How we categorize tool calls

Tool call categories and included activities Category Includes Image Viewing

Original images; crops and other processed views

Cropping; zooming/resizing; rotation; contrast/brightness adjustments; annotations and guides; masks/false colors; ASCII renderings

Object counts; areas; band intensities; intensity profiles; coordinates; distances; structural relationships; plots of measurements

Comments; empty code; static narration or reasoning

- OCR: text and label extraction from pixels

- Calculation: numerical, statistical, symbolic, or scientific calculations

- Inspection/setup: files, dimensions, metadata, dependencies, saved results, helper scripts

- Answer writing: final answer file creation, formatting, readback

- Other/unclear: uncategorized activity or insufficient evidence

One primary category per call, based on its main activity.

Image viewing comes from the view_image tool; the other activity groups classify code_exec calls. Other includes file and environment inspection, answer writing, calculation, OCR, and unclear activity. OCR accounts for 12.4% of Other calls; Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) accounts for 21% of OCR calls.

### Not every code execution does analysis

Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) accounts for 86.7% of the cohort’s calls classified as commentary/no-op . This represents 5.6% of its tool calls, or about 3.8 of its 67.5 calls per task.

commentary/no-op tool calls cover static narration, comments, or printed text without new computation or file analysis. In Protein spot 22, a commentary/no-op tool call prints an interpretation of the spot labels. The code execution tool acts as a notepad: the model writes out its interpretation and the text returns in the next model request.

## More intelligent models tend to call fewer tools

Models with higher Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores generally make fewer tool calls on VIALS-AA.

But similar VIALS-AA scores can come from very different inspection strategies: Opus and Sonnet make substantially more tool calls and image measurements than Astra and Sol.

### VIALS-AA: Tool Use vs. Intelligence

Each point is one model across the same 161 tasks and three independent repeats

## Models solve similar numbers of tasks, but top scorers are far more consistent

Leading open weights models solve about as many tasks at least once as closed frontier models, but are much less consistent. Kimi K3.1 Pro (max), MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (max) each solve 114–119 tasks at least once, against 111–118 for the seven top-scoring models, all closed. They pass all three repeats on only 48–73 tasks, against 95–103. Our headline metric, pass3, is the share of tasks answered correctly in all three repeats. We use pass3 because inconsistent answers in scientific work can lead to wrong conclusions and costly follow-up experiments.

### VIALS-AA: Consistency Across Three Repeats

Share of tasks passing zero, one, two, or all three repeats

## Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads in three of eight domains

Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads or shares the lead in three of the eight domain groups: plasmid maps, phylogenetics, and flow cytometry. It shares the flow-cytometry lead with Gemini 4 Argon (high). Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads on blotting, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) on cell counting, and GPT-6.1 Terra (max) on protein structure/binding. GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) share the lead on molecular structure.

### VIALS-AA: Score by Domain

Share of tasks answered correctly in all three repeats by scientific domain. Colors are normalized within each domain across all models tested

## Cost per Task varies by nearly 100× across models

Cost per task ranges from 0.02 for GPT-6 Luna (max) to 1.77 for Grok 4.7 (xhigh), a 99 × spread. GPT-6.1 Sol (max) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) score 59% and 60% , respectively, but Sonnet costs about 18 × as much per task.

Output tokens per task range from about 2.21k for GPT-6 Astra (max) to 94.6k for MiMo-V2.6-Pro, a 43 × spread. Reasoning makes up most of each model’s output. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) uses 63.5k , including 54.6k reasoning tokens: about 25 × as many output tokens as GPT-6.1 Sol (max) for a similar score.

### Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Small: the highest scoring open weights model outside of China pending weights release

Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index - their plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings

### Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B scoring 20 on the Intelligence Index

Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B, an open weights model matching Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with stronger terminal use but weaker knowledge

### Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5

Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

summaryZh: # VIALS-AA：科学图像推理的不同路径 VIALS-AA 是我们对 Handshake AI 的 VIALS 基准的实现，测试语言模型是否可以解释科学图像并回答有关其所包含证据的问题。模型会采取不同的路径来获得正确答案，即使在广泛检查图像后，模型也经常会提出错误的问题。
